stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 34 year old G3P2 at 30+2 weeks presents with a sudden gush of bright red vaginal blood soaking through a pad. She reports no pain and the baby has been moving normally. Both previous births were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries.

She has had no antenatal care since the dating scan at 12 weeks after moving from interstate. She is Rhesus positive with no known medical problems and takes no regular medications.

On examination she is anxious but comfortable. Her abdomen is soft and non tender with a longitudinal lie and cephalic presentation. Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 128/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, foetal heart rate 145 with reactive CTG. Speculum examination has not yet been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen; longitudinal lie; cephalic; blood pooling on pad
data_table.Obstetric history: G3P2, two prior uncomplicated vaginal births; no antenatal care beyond 12 week dating scan
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold sent; FBC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Immediate digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation and station
options.rationale: Digital examination is contraindicated in undiagnosed antepartum haemorrhage until placental site is confirmed because a finger through a low lying placenta can precipitate torrential bleeding (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta before any vaginal examination
options.rationale: Painless bright red bleeding in the third trimester without prior placental localisation mandates transvaginal ultrasound before any digital examination; transvaginal is safe in placenta praevia and more accurate than transabdominal alone for the lower segment (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Bedside Kleihauer Betke test to quantify foetomaternal haemorrhage before any imaging
options.rationale: Kleihauer is used to guide anti D dose in Rhesus negative women and to detect foetomaternal haemorrhage; it does not localise the placenta and this woman is Rhesus positive (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Speculum examination first to identify a local cervical or vaginal source of bleeding
options.rationale: Speculum examination is safe in praevia but ultrasound localisation is the higher priority next step because it changes the entire pathway including mode of delivery, whereas speculum only identifies incidental cervical lesions (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: MRI pelvis with placental accreta spectrum protocol before any bedside assessment is done
options.rationale: MRI has a role for suspected accreta after ultrasound suggests praevia over a prior caesarean scar; it is not the initial investigation in an actively bleeding woman with no confirmed praevia (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum).

explanation.summary: Undiagnosed antepartum haemorrhage requires placental localisation before any digital or invasive assessment. Painless bright red bleeding at 30+ weeks is classically praevia until proven otherwise; abruption is classically painful with a tense uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and more accurate than transabdominal for the lower segment. Digital examination through an unrecognised praevia can precipitate catastrophic bleeding.
key_points: Painless third trimester bleeding suggests praevia.
Never perform digital examination before placental localisation.
Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and preferred in suspected praevia.
explanation.pearls: In any woman with antepartum bleeding whose placental site is not documented, transvaginal ultrasound is safe and precedes digital or speculum examination.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia
RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption recognition and delivery timing
stem:
You are the on call registrar. A 29 year old G2P1 at 34+5 weeks presents after a low speed motor vehicle collision one hour ago. She was the belted front seat passenger. She describes constant severe lower abdominal pain and reduced foetal movements since the crash.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated. Anti D at 28 weeks was given because she is Rhesus negative. She takes no other medications.

On examination she is pale and clammy. Abdomen is rigid and exquisitely tender with a woody consistency to the uterus. There is a small amount of dark blood at the introitus. Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 88/52, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% room air, temp 36.4, foetal heart rate 90 with recurrent late decelerations on CTG. Bedside ultrasound shows a posterior fundal placenta with no praevia and no retroplacental clot visualised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 88/52, RR 24, SpO2 97% room air, temp 36.4, FHR 90 with recurrent late decelerations
data_table.Examination: Pale clammy; woody rigid tender abdomen; small dark blood at introitus
data_table.Imaging: Bedside USS: posterior fundal placenta, no praevia, no retroplacental clot seen
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1 at 34+5, Rhesus negative, anti D at 28 weeks given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer by road to a tertiary centre 90 minutes away for management with specialist input
options.rationale: Interfacility transfer with active abruption, shock and foetal bradycardia is unsafe; delivery must occur locally with concurrent maternal resuscitation (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Admit for continuous CTG monitoring and betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular for 48 hours
options.rationale: Expectant management is inappropriate with maternal haemodynamic instability and non reassuring CTG; awaiting steroid effect risks stillbirth and maternal disseminated intravascular coagulation (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Repeat formal ultrasound to look for retroplacental clot before deciding on operative delivery
options.rationale: Ultrasound is insensitive for abruption with false negative rate around 50%; withholding delivery to await imaging in a shocked woman with a bradycardic foetus is unsafe (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin E2 and augment with oxytocin for expected rapid delivery
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery may be considered in stable abruption with dead foetus or reassuring foetal status; this foetus is alive with bradycardia and the mother is shocked so caesarean is required now (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section with concurrent maternal resuscitation and massive transfusion activation
options.rationale: Maternal shock plus a foetal heart rate of 90 with recurrent late decelerations in the context of trauma and a woody uterus signals abruption with foetal compromise; category 1 birth within 30 minutes with concurrent transfusion is required regardless of the absence of retroplacental clot on ultrasound (ultrasound is insensitive for abruption) (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Placental abruption after trauma presents with pain, a tense woody uterus, and foetal compromise. Vaginal bleeding may be minimal or absent because blood collects behind the placenta. Ultrasound sensitivity is around 50%, so a negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis. Category 1 caesarean with concurrent resuscitation is indicated when the mother is unstable or the foetus is compromised.
key_points: Ultrasound has 50% sensitivity for abruption.
Maternal shock plus foetal bradycardia mandates category 1 caesarean.
Concealed abruption may bleed heavily internally with little external blood.
explanation.pearls: Placental abruption is a clinical diagnosis; a negative ultrasound never excludes it and never delays delivery when the foetus or mother is compromised.

sources.label: RCOG Green top guideline 63 Antepartum haemorrhage

stem:
You are the on call registrar in a rural birth centre. A 32 year old G1 at 37+3 weeks was admitted for expectant management of a bilobed placenta with a low lying accessory lobe noted on the 32 week scan. Follow up scan at 36 weeks was not performed because of geography.

Her waters broke spontaneously 10 minutes ago with a small amount of fresh red blood immediately following the gush of clear liquor. She reports no pain.

She is alert and comfortable. Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8. The CTG that had been reassuring five minutes ago now shows a sudden onset foetal heart rate of 70 with a sinusoidal pattern. Abdomen is soft and non tender. The presenting part is high and not engaged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.8
data_table.CTG: Sudden foetal bradycardia to 70 with sinusoidal pattern immediately after SROM
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen; presenting part high and not engaged; small volume fresh red vaginal blood post SROM
data_table.Antenatal imaging: 32 week USS bilobed placenta with low lying accessory lobe; 36 week follow up not performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section immediately with paediatric team on standby for neonatal transfusion
options.rationale: Painless fresh vaginal bleeding at membrane rupture with acute foetal bradycardia and a sinusoidal CTG in a woman with a bilobed placenta and unassessed accessory lobe is vasa praevia until proven otherwise; the bleeding is foetal, exsanguination is rapid, and category 1 caesarean with neonatal transfusion readiness is the only option (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Continuous CTG for 30 minutes to see if the foetal heart rate recovers before deciding on birth mode
options.rationale: Vasa praevia has a foetal blood volume of about 80 to 100 mL total so exsanguination occurs in minutes; watchful CTG loses the child (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Perform an urgent Apt test on the vaginal blood to distinguish foetal from maternal haemoglobin
options.rationale: The Apt test is historically used to differentiate foetal from maternal blood but takes time and does not change management here; the CTG confirms foetal compromise and delivery must not wait for laboratory confirmation (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Instrumental vaginal birth with a Kiwi cup once cervix is confirmed fully dilated on examination
options.rationale: Instrumental birth requires full dilatation and engaged head; the presenting part is high and cervix is not fully dilated so this is not feasible and cannot occur in time (Source: RANZCOG Instrumental vaginal birth).

options.text: Amnioinfusion with warmed normal saline to relieve presumed cord compression from oligohydramnios
options.rationale: Amnioinfusion is used for recurrent variable decelerations from oligohydramnios; this pattern is a sinusoidal trace with bleeding after SROM which is foetal haemorrhage, not cord compression (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum foetal surveillance).

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is the presence of foetal vessels traversing the membranes over the internal os, unsupported by placenta or cord. Risk factors include bilobed or succenturiate placenta, velamentous cord insertion, low lying placenta at second trimester scan, and IVF pregnancy. Membrane rupture tears the vessels causing foetal exsanguination within minutes. A sinusoidal CTG immediately after SROM with fresh vaginal blood is pathognomonic and mandates category 1 caesarean with neonatal transfusion readiness.
key_points: Sinusoidal CTG plus bleeding after SROM equals vasa praevia.
Foetal blood volume is small so exsanguination is rapid.
Bilobed and succenturiate lobe placentae are high risk.
explanation.pearls: In known bilobed placenta with low lying accessory lobe, plan elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with antenatal steroids because emergency SROM after 37 weeks kills the foetus in minutes.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

stem:
You are the birthing suite registrar. A 27 year old G1 at 29+4 weeks presents with regular painful uterine contractions every 4 minutes for the past two hours. Speculum reveals no liquor and no bleeding.

Her pregnancy has been complicated by chronic hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily. There is no history of asthma, cardiac disease, or diabetes. She takes only labetalol and a pregnancy multivitamin.

On examination her abdomen is soft between contractions and non tender. The cervix is 3 cm dilated and 80% effaced. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 148/92, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, foetal heart rate 145 reactive. Foetal fibronectin is not available. Betamethasone has already been given and magnesium sulfate infusion for neuroprotection has been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 148/92, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80% effaced; soft non tender abdomen between contractions
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg BD; pregnancy multivitamin; betamethasone given; magnesium sulfate infusion running
data_table.Obstetric history: G1 at 29+4; no membrane rupture; no bleeding; no diabetes or asthma

lead_in: Which agent is most appropriate for tocolysis?

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally as a loading dose then 20 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours
options.rationale: Nifedipine is the usual first line tocolytic in Australia but concurrent intravenous magnesium plus nifedipine can cause profound hypotension and neuromuscular blockade so the combination is avoided when magnesium is already running (Source: RANZCOG Tocolysis in preterm labour).

options.text: Salbutamol intravenous infusion titrated to a maternal pulse under 120 beats per minute
options.rationale: Beta agonist tocolysis is no longer recommended in Australia because of maternal cardiac side effects and pulmonary oedema; contraindicated in chronic hypertension (Source: RANZCOG Tocolysis in preterm labour).

options.text: Atosiban intravenous 6.75 mg bolus then infusion at 300 mcg per minute for 3 hours
options.rationale: Atosiban is an oxytocin receptor antagonist with equivalent efficacy to nifedipine but is not available on the PBS in Australia and is not stocked in most Australian units (Source: RANZCOG Tocolysis in preterm labour).

options.text: Indomethacin 100 mg rectally then 50 mg orally every 6 hours for up to 48 hours
options.rationale: With magnesium already infusing and a woman on labetalol for hypertension, indomethacin is the preferred tocolytic because it avoids the calcium channel blocker plus magnesium interaction; use is limited to under 32 weeks and under 48 hours because of oligohydramnios and ductal constriction beyond that window, both of which apply here (Source: RANZCOG Tocolysis in preterm labour).

options.text: Additional intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus followed by 2 g per hour for tocolysis
options.rationale: Magnesium is used for neuroprotection under 30 weeks but is not an effective tocolytic in current evidence and increasing the dose risks maternal toxicity (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection).

explanation.summary: Tocolysis buys 48 hours for steroid effect and in utero transfer. First line in Australia is nifedipine, second line indomethacin under 32 weeks for up to 48 hours. Nifedipine and magnesium co administration risks profound hypotension and should be avoided. Beta agonists are obsolete. Atosiban is not on the PBS. Magnesium itself is not an effective tocolytic though it is given for neuroprotection under 30 weeks.
key_points: Nifedipine first line but not with concurrent magnesium.
Indomethacin allowed under 32 weeks for up to 48 hours.
Magnesium for neuroprotection is separate from tocolysis.
explanation.pearls: Indomethacin tocolysis is bounded by two clocks: gestation under 32 weeks and duration under 48 hours; beyond either the ductal constriction and oligohydramnios risks outweigh benefit.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 31 year old G2P1 at 28+6 weeks with confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 6 hours ago now has regular contractions every 3 minutes.

Her previous birth was a term vaginal delivery. Antenatal group B streptococcus screen is unknown. She takes no medications and has no allergies.

On examination her abdomen contracts palpably every 3 minutes and is non tender between. Speculum confirms pooling of clear liquor at the cervix. Cervix is 4 cm dilated. Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, foetal heart rate 150 reactive. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular was given 3 hours ago. Intrapartum benzylpenicillin has been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, FHR 150 reactive
data_table.Examination: Contractions every 3 min; cervix 4 cm dilated; pooling clear liquor
data_table.Medications: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 3 h ago; intrapartum benzylpenicillin commenced
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1 at 28+6; prior term vaginal birth; GBS status unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose then 1 g per hour for neuroprotection
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection is indicated for imminent preterm birth under 30 weeks; standard regimen is 4 g loading over 20 to 30 minutes then 1 g per hour, ideally starting at least 4 hours before delivery and continuing for up to 24 hours or until birth (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection).

options.text: Second dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular immediately to complete the loading regimen early
options.rationale: The second betamethasone dose is given 24 hours after the first; giving it early does not accelerate lung maturation and is not recommended (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal corticosteroids).

options.text: Add clindamycin intravenous to cover intrapartum GBS pending laboratory swab result
options.rationale: Clindamycin is used for GBS prophylaxis only in penicillin allergic women with severe reactions and confirmed clindamycin susceptibility; benzylpenicillin is already appropriate and adding clindamycin is not indicated (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis).

options.text: Commence nifedipine 20 mg orally as tocolysis to delay birth by a further 48 hours if possible
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in established preterm labour with rupture of membranes and cervical dilatation of 4 cm because progression is not preventable; effort is redirected to neuroprotection and transfer (Source: RANZCOG Tocolysis in preterm labour).

options.text: Perform emergency category 2 caesarean section on the basis of possible intrauterine infection now
options.rationale: There is no fever or maternal or foetal tachycardia to suggest chorioamnionitis; caesarean under 30 weeks in labour without clear indication increases morbidity (Source: RANZCOG Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate reduces the risk of cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in preterm survivors when given before imminent birth under 30 weeks. The Australian standard is 4 g loading then 1 g per hour. Steroids have already been commenced. GBS prophylaxis with benzylpenicillin is standard when status is unknown and labour is under 37 weeks. Tocolysis is not indicated once labour is established with cervical change and ruptured membranes.
key_points: Magnesium neuroprotection is for imminent birth under 30 weeks.
Loading 4 g, maintenance 1 g per hour.
Unknown GBS status under 37 weeks equals intrapartum benzylpenicillin.
explanation.pearls: Australian magnesium neuroprotection is a 4 g load then 1 g per hour, ideally at least 4 hours before birth; benefit does not extend past 30+0 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

stem:
You are the labour ward registrar. A 34 year old G3P2 at 36+2 weeks presents in early labour with contractions every 5 minutes. Her antenatal vaginal rectal swab at 35 weeks grew group B streptococcus.

She has a documented severe reaction to penicillin during a previous UTI treatment: throat swelling, wheeze, and required adrenaline. Antibiotic susceptibility testing on the GBS isolate shows resistance to clindamycin.

On examination her abdomen is soft between contractions and non tender. Cervix is 3 cm dilated and 60% effaced. Membranes are intact. Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, foetal heart rate 140 reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, FHR 140 reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated 60% effaced; membranes intact; soft non tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: 35 week GBS swab positive; isolate clindamycin resistant
data_table.Allergies: Penicillin: throat swelling, wheeze, required adrenaline

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic is most appropriate?

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is first line for GBS prophylaxis but is absolutely contraindicated in a woman with a prior severe immediate reaction requiring adrenaline (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis).

options.text: Cefazolin 2 g intravenous loading then 1 g every 8 hours until birth
options.rationale: Cefazolin is the alternative for penicillin allergy that is NOT severe immediate hypersensitivity; the anaphylactoid history here means cephalosporins carry cross reactivity risk and are not used (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis).

options.text: Clindamycin 900 mg intravenous every 8 hours until birth for penicillin allergic women
options.rationale: Clindamycin is the choice for severe penicillin allergy ONLY when the isolate is susceptible; this isolate is clindamycin resistant so vancomycin is required (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis).

options.text: Vancomycin 20 mg per kg intravenous every 8 hours (maximum 2 g per dose) until birth
options.rationale: For women with severe immediate penicillin hypersensitivity AND clindamycin resistant GBS, intrapartum vancomycin is the recommended agent per ANZCOG and CDC criteria (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis).

options.text: Erythromycin 500 mg intravenous every 6 hours until birth as an alternative macrolide
options.rationale: Erythromycin is no longer recommended for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis because of poor foetal serum penetration and rising resistance (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis).

explanation.summary: GBS prophylaxis selects agent by both maternal allergy severity and isolate susceptibility. Non severe penicillin allergy allows cefazolin. Severe immediate hypersensitivity with clindamycin susceptible isolate uses clindamycin. Severe hypersensitivity plus resistant isolate uses vancomycin. Erythromycin is dropped from current recommendations because of poor foetal transfer and resistance.
key_points: Severe penicillin allergy plus clindamycin resistance equals vancomycin.
Cefazolin is only for non severe penicillin allergy.
Erythromycin is no longer used.
explanation.pearls: The GBS second line ladder is cefazolin for mild penicillin allergy, clindamycin only if susceptible, and vancomycin when neither is safe or effective.

sources.label: CDC Prevention of Perinatal Group B Streptococcal Disease

stem:
You are the antenatal GP registrar. A 30 year old G2P1 at 26 weeks attends for review of her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed after an overnight fast.

She has a BMI of 24 with no family history of diabetes. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a birth weight of 3.4 kg at term. She takes only pregnancy multivitamins.

Examination is unremarkable. Symphysis fundal height is appropriate for gestation and blood pressure is 118/72. The pathology report shows fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L, one hour glucose 10.4 mmol/L, and two hour glucose 8.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72; other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: SFH appropriate for 26 weeks; foetal movements normal
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 4.9 mmol/L, 1 h 10.4 mmol/L, 2 h 8.2 mmol/L
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1, prior term vaginal birth, birth weight 3.4 kg

lead_in: How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Normal result with all three values below the ADIPS diagnostic thresholds for pregnancy
options.rationale: The one hour value of 10.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS one hour threshold of 10.0 mmol/L; a single elevated value on any of the three time points diagnoses gestational diabetes (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Gestational diabetes based on a one hour value at or above the diagnostic threshold
options.rationale: ADIPS diagnostic thresholds after 75 g OGTT in pregnancy are fasting at or above 5.1, one hour at or above 10.0, or two hour at or above 8.5; a single value at or above threshold is diagnostic and the one hour of 10.4 is above cut off (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Impaired glucose tolerance requiring a repeat test in four weeks to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: There is no impaired glucose tolerance category within the ADIPS pregnancy schema; a single value above threshold is gestational diabetes and repeat testing is not required (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Overt diabetes in pregnancy given the elevated one hour and two hour glucose measurements
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy is diagnosed by fasting at or above 7.0, HbA1c at or above 6.5%, or random at or above 11.1; these criteria are not met so the diagnosis is gestational diabetes not overt (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Result inconclusive because at least two values must be above threshold for a diagnosis
options.rationale: Two out of three abnormal values is the older WHO 1999 rule; the current ADIPS and WHO 2013 rule requires only one abnormal value (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

explanation.summary: The Australian ADIPS diagnostic thresholds on a 75 g OGTT in pregnancy are fasting at or above 5.1, one hour at or above 10.0, and two hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L. A single value at or above threshold makes the diagnosis. Overt diabetes in pregnancy uses higher cut offs and identifies women likely to have pre existing type 2 disease. Repeat testing is not part of the diagnostic pathway.
key_points: ADIPS diagnostic values: 5.1 fasting, 10.0 one hour, 8.5 two hour.
One value equals diagnosis in current criteria.
Overt DM in pregnancy uses higher fasting and HbA1c cut offs.
explanation.pearls: Remember 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 as the ADIPS trio; the one hour value at exactly 10.0 already makes the diagnosis, and 10.4 leaves no ambiguity.

sources.label: ADIPS consensus guidelines for testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes
RANZCOG Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

stem:
You are the antenatal diabetes registrar. A 33 year old G2P1 at 32 weeks with gestational diabetes was commenced on metformin 500 mg twice daily four weeks ago after two weeks of failed dietary control. She has titrated up to 1 g twice daily over the past fortnight.

She is otherwise well with no other medical conditions. She is compliant with the diet and self monitoring diary. There is no infection or steroid use.

Examination is unremarkable. Symphysis fundal height measures 36 cm at 32 weeks and the last growth scan two weeks ago showed abdominal circumference on the 92nd centile with an estimated foetal weight on the 88th centile. Her home blood glucose diary over the past week shows fasting values averaging 5.8 mmol/L and two hour post prandial values averaging 8.4 mmol/L, with most values above target.

data_table.Investigations: USS at 30 weeks: AC 92nd centile, EFW 88th centile
data_table.Blood glucose diary: Fasting mean 5.8 mmol/L; 2 h post prandial mean 8.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD titrated over 2 weeks; no steroids; no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to management?

options.text: Add long acting isophane insulin at bedtime and short acting insulin with meals as needed
options.rationale: Australian targets are fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and two hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L; failure to reach targets on maximally tolerated metformin combined with foetal macrosomia signs mandates addition of insulin, typically basal at bedtime for elevated fasting values and prandial short acting for elevated post prandial values (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy

options.text: Increase metformin to 1 g in the morning and 1.5 g at night to reach the maximal dose
options.rationale: Maximal metformin in pregnancy is 2 g per day; she is already at that dose and gastrointestinal tolerability limits pushing higher, so insulin is required (Source: AMH; ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy

options.text: Commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg orally in the morning in addition to current metformin
options.rationale: Glibenclamide crosses the placenta and is associated with higher rates of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia; it is not recommended in Australia for GDM (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy

options.text: Refer to the dietitian for a stricter low carbohydrate meal plan and repeat review in one week
options.rationale: She is already dietary compliant and macrosomia is developing; further delay of pharmacotherapy risks continued foetal overgrowth (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy

options.text: Bring forward induction of labour to 37 weeks to reduce the risk of stillbirth and shoulder dystocia
options.rationale: Timing of birth in GDM depends on control; well controlled GDM on diet delivers by 40+6, on medication by 39+6, and poor control considers 38 to 39; treatment optimisation precedes preterm induction (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

explanation.summary: GDM management steps up from diet to metformin to insulin. Australian home targets are fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and two hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L. Persistent readings above target on maximal metformin, or emerging macrosomia, are the trigger for insulin. Glibenclamide is not used in Australia. Timing of birth depends on control quality; well controlled diet only can go to 40+6, medicated to 39+6.
key_points: Targets: fasting under 5.0, two hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L.
Maximal metformin is 2 g per day.
Insulin is added when targets missed on metformin or macrosomia emerges.
explanation.pearls: Fasting hyperglycaemia gets bedtime basal insulin; post prandial hyperglycaemia gets prandial rapid acting; targets 5.0 fasting and 6.7 at two hours are the Australian numbers to memorise.

sources.label: ADIPS consensus guidelines for the management of gestational diabetes in pregnancy
RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

subtopic_detail: Timing of delivery in insulin treated GDM
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar. A 36 year old G3P2 with gestational diabetes on insulin presents at 38+3 weeks. Her diabetes has been well controlled since insulin started at 30 weeks with fasting values averaging 4.6 mmol/L and post prandial values averaging 6.3 mmol/L.

Both previous births were normal vaginal deliveries at 39 and 40 weeks with birth weights of 3.7 and 3.9 kg. She has no other medical problems.

Examination is unremarkable. Symphysis fundal height at today's visit is 39 cm. Growth scan two weeks ago showed abdominal circumference on the 65th centile and estimated foetal weight on the 60th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery Doppler. Blood pressure is 118/72.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72; other observations within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: USS at 36+3: AC 65th centile, EFW 60th centile, AFI normal, UA Doppler normal
data_table.Blood glucose diary: Fasting mean 4.6 mmol/L; 2 h post prandial mean 6.3 mmol/L; on insulin since 30 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing of birth?

options.text: Await spontaneous labour up to 40+6 weeks with weekly antenatal review and growth surveillance
options.rationale: Awaiting 40+6 is appropriate for diet controlled GDM with normal foetal growth; women on insulin have a higher stillbirth risk and are offered birth by 39+6 (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

options.text: Continue expectant management until 41+0 weeks then discuss induction of labour options
options.rationale: Insulin treated GDM does not proceed to 41 weeks because of stillbirth risk; the recommended window is up to 39+6 (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean section this week for macrosomia prevention and safer maternal outcome
options.rationale: Foetal weight is on the 60th centile with no macrosomia; caesarean is offered for estimated foetal weight above 4.5 kg in GDM per RANZCOG, not for well controlled GDM with normal growth (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

options.text: Offer induction of labour immediately given the SFH of 39 cm suggests foetal macrosomia now
options.rationale: SFH alone is not reliable at this gestation; ultrasound weight on the 60th centile two weeks ago excludes macrosomia and does not justify immediate induction (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

options.text: Offer induction of labour between 39+0 and 39+6 weeks with balloon or prostaglandin cervical priming
options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends offering birth to insulin treated GDM between 39+0 and 39+6 to balance stillbirth risk against neonatal morbidity from earlier birth; method depends on Bishop score, with balloon or prostaglandin for unfavourable cervix (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and treatment of gestational diabetes

explanation.summary: Timing of birth in GDM stratifies by treatment and control. Diet controlled with normal growth can go to 40+6 or await labour. Medication treated GDM is offered birth between 39+0 and 39+6. Poor control considers 38 to 39. Caesarean is not routine unless estimated foetal weight is above 4.5 kg or other indication exists.
key_points: Diet controlled GDM up to 40+6.
Medication treated GDM by 39+6.
Caesarean offered if EFW over 4.5 kg.
explanation.pearls: The 39+6 ceiling in insulin treated GDM reflects a rising stillbirth curve after 40 weeks despite normal growth and normal Dopplers.

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacological choice with fertility desire
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 32 year old woman presents with heavy periods for the past 8 months. She soaks a super pad hourly on her heaviest two days and passes 50 cent piece sized clots.

Her cycle is regular at 28 days lasting 8 days. She is trying to conceive with her partner and has been trying for 3 months. She is otherwise well with no medications or allergies.

Examination is normal including bimanual pelvic examination with a mobile normal sized uterus and no adnexal masses. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal endometrium at 6 mm and no fibroids or polyps. Full blood count reveals haemoglobin 105 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 74 fL (80 to 100), and ferritin 8 microgram/L (15 to 200). Thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Bimanual normal; mobile normal sized uterus; no adnexal mass
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic USS: endometrium 6 mm; no fibroid or polyp
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105 g/L (115-165); MCV 74 fL (80-100); ferritin 8 mcg/L (15-200); TFTs and coags normal
data_table.Fertility: Actively trying to conceive for 3 months

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system inserted at the next menstrual period
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective pharmacological option for heavy menstrual bleeding but is contraceptive; it is not appropriate for a woman actively trying to conceive (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with 30 mcg ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel continuously
options.rationale: The combined oral contraceptive is effective for heavy menstrual bleeding but suppresses ovulation and prevents conception, which is contrary to the patient's goals (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily during menstruation for the duration of bleeding days
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is a first line non hormonal treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding with idiopathic ovulatory HMB and preserves fertility; it reduces blood loss by around 40% without affecting conception (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Norethisterone 5 mg orally three times daily from day 5 to day 26 of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Cyclical norethisterone from day 5 to 26 suppresses ovulation and functions as contraception at that dose and schedule, which is contrary to fertility intentions (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Referral for endometrial ablation because pharmacological therapy is unlikely to be adequate long term
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation destroys endometrium and is a permanent contraceptive method; it is contraindicated when future pregnancy is desired (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding workup covers PALM COEIN structural causes, pregnancy, and coagulation. When structural, systemic, and endocrine causes are excluded and fertility is desired, tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid are the first line options because both preserve conception. TXA reduces loss by around 40%, mefenamic acid by 30%. Iron deficiency anaemia is treated in parallel.
key_points: PALM COEIN excludes structural and systemic causes.
TXA and mefenamic acid preserve fertility.
Mirena, COCP, cyclical progestogens and ablation all preclude pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: In a woman with heavy menstrual bleeding trying to conceive, tranexamic acid at 1 g three times daily during menses is first line; add iron and treat the ferritin under 30.

subtopic_detail: Structural cause workup with intermenstrual bleeding
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 44 year old parous woman is referred by her GP with heavy menstrual bleeding for 12 months and new intermenstrual bleeding for 3 months. Cervical screening is up to date and negative.

Her cycle is regular at 28 days and cycles typically last 9 days. She has completed her family and uses condoms for contraception. She has no bleeding diathesis and no medications.

Bimanual examination is normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterus with endometrial thickness of 14 mm and a discrete 12 mm hyperechoic focus at the fundus with a feeder vessel on colour Doppler. Full blood count reveals haemoglobin 108 g/L (115 to 165) with normal indices.

data_table.Examination: Bimanual normal; uterus normal size and mobile
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: endometrium 14 mm; 12 mm hyperechoic fundal focus with feeder vessel on colour Doppler
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L (115-165); MCV within normal limits; cervical screen up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to see if the lesion resolves spontaneously
options.rationale: A discrete hyperechoic lesion with a feeder vessel is characteristic of an endometrial polyp and does not resolve spontaneously; deferring investigation delays histological diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

options.text: Blind endometrial Pipelle biopsy in the clinic as the primary tissue sampling strategy
options.rationale: Pipelle is a blind sample that misses focal lesions such as polyps in around half of cases; when a focal lesion is seen on imaging, directed hysteroscopic sampling is required (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

options.text: Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and polypectomy of the focal lesion under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: A focal endometrial lesion with feeder vessel on ultrasound plus intermenstrual bleeding requires hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and polypectomy; blind sampling misses focal lesions and the polyp needs excision for both diagnosis and treatment (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

options.text: Pelvic MRI with contrast to characterise the focal lesion before deciding further investigation
options.rationale: MRI is used for suspected adenomyosis or complex fibroid mapping before myomectomy; it does not provide histology and adds no information beyond the diagnostic ultrasound here (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

options.text: Commence tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menstruation and reassess in three months
options.rationale: Empirical pharmacotherapy without tissue diagnosis is unsafe when a focal lesion is present in a 44 year old with intermenstrual bleeding; malignancy must be excluded first (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding with intermenstrual bleeding raises suspicion for a structural cause. Transvaginal ultrasound with saline infusion or a good quality standard scan localises focal lesions such as polyps and submucosal fibroids. Blind Pipelle sampling misses focal lesions in around half of cases. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the gold standard when a focal lesion is seen and allows concurrent polypectomy.
key_points: Focal lesion on TVUS equals hysteroscopy with directed biopsy.
Pipelle is blind and misses focal disease.
Intermenstrual bleeding raises malignancy suspicion at any age but especially over 45.
explanation.pearls: A hyperechoic focus with a single feeder vessel on colour Doppler is the classic ultrasound signature of an endometrial polyp; take it to hysteroscopy, not a Pipelle.

sources.label: RANZCOG Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 62 year old woman presents with a single episode of light pink vaginal bleeding two days ago. Her last menstrual period was at age 52 and she has had no bleeding since.

She is otherwise well with a BMI of 34, well controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin, and hypertension on perindopril. She has never used hormone therapy. Cervical screening is up to date and negative.

Examination reveals no vulval or vaginal lesion on speculum. Bimanual examination is normal with a small mobile uterus and no adnexal masses. Urgent transvaginal ultrasound performed the same week reports a homogenous endometrial thickness of 6 mm with no focal lesion and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: No vulvovaginal lesion on speculum; bimanual normal; small mobile uterus
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: endometrium 6 mm homogenous; no focal lesion; no free fluid
data_table.Past history: BMI 34; T2DM on metformin; hypertension on perindopril; never used HRT

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and review only if further bleeding episodes occur in the next six months
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness above 4 mm requires tissue sampling because ultrasound alone cannot exclude endometrial cancer above this threshold (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to see if the endometrial thickness reduces below 4 mm
options.rationale: The endometrium does not remodel after menopause and the 4 mm cut off is a single measurement threshold; repeat imaging delays tissue diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Commence topical vaginal oestrogen and review response over the next three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen is used for atrophic vaginitis after malignancy has been excluded; sampling is required first with an endometrial thickness of 6 mm (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Endometrial Pipelle biopsy in the outpatient setting with hysteroscopy if inadequate or negative
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness above 4 mm mandates endometrial sampling; outpatient Pipelle is the first line sample and hysteroscopy follows if the sample is inadequate, non diagnostic, or bleeding recurs (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Refer directly to gynaecological oncology for total abdominal hysterectomy after preoperative workup
options.rationale: Definitive surgery follows histological diagnosis of endometrial cancer; proceeding to hysterectomy without histology is not appropriate (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Transvaginal ultrasound with an endometrial thickness at or under 4 mm has a high negative predictive value and allows conservative watchful waiting. Above 4 mm, tissue sampling is required. First line is outpatient Pipelle; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is used when Pipelle is inadequate, non diagnostic, or bleeding recurs. Obesity, unopposed oestrogen exposure, T2DM and tamoxifen use raise the pretest probability.
key_points: PMB with ET over 4 mm equals endometrial sampling.
Pipelle first, hysteroscopy for inadequate or recurrent PMB.
Obesity, T2DM and unopposed oestrogen raise risk.
explanation.pearls: The 4 mm cut off on TVUS in postmenopausal bleeding is a rule out; anything thicker or unable to visualise clearly gets biopsied regardless of imaging appearance.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Endometrial cancer optimal care pathway

stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 68 year old woman presents to your clinic with her third episode of postmenopausal bleeding in eight weeks. Her first two episodes were investigated by her GP with transvaginal ultrasound each time showing an endometrial thickness of 3 mm and Pipelle sampling that returned scant benign endometrial tissue.

She has a BMI of 41, type 2 diabetes on metformin, and previously took tamoxifen for five years following breast cancer at age 55. Cervical screening is up to date.

Examination reveals atrophic vulvovaginal changes with no discrete lesion. Bimanual examination is normal. Repeat transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm with a poorly seen endometrial midline echo and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (115 to 165).

data_table.Examination: Atrophic vulvovaginal changes; no discrete lesion; bimanual normal
data_table.Imaging: TVUS today: ET 3 mm with poorly seen midline echo; small free fluid in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (115-165); prior 2 Pipelle samples: scant benign endometrium
data_table.Past history: BMI 41; T2DM on metformin; prior tamoxifen 5 years for breast cancer age 55

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that thin endometrium excludes malignancy and review in three months if symptoms persist
options.rationale: The 4 mm cut off only rules out malignancy on the first presentation; recurrent postmenopausal bleeding regardless of endometrial thickness requires further investigation because a thin endometrium does not reliably exclude cancer in this setting (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy under general anaesthesia to obtain a definitive histological sample
options.rationale: Recurrent postmenopausal bleeding despite thin endometrium and inadequate Pipelle sampling, in a woman with multiple risk factors including prior tamoxifen, poor midline echo visualisation and free fluid mandates hysteroscopy with directed biopsy because focal lesions and sub endometrial pathology are missed by blind sampling (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Third Pipelle biopsy in the clinic with concurrent saline infusion sonohysterography for guidance
options.rationale: Repeating a blind Pipelle after two inadequate samples adds little; the appropriate escalation is direct visualisation with hysteroscopy (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Commence topical vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophic vaginitis and review response over six weeks
options.rationale: Atrophic vaginitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in postmenopausal bleeding; recurrent bleeding with tamoxifen exposure and inadequate sampling mandates hysteroscopy before symptomatic treatment (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: MRI pelvis with contrast to stage a presumed malignancy prior to any further tissue sampling
options.rationale: Staging imaging follows histological diagnosis of malignancy; no histology exists yet so tissue must come first (Source: Cancer Council Australia Endometrial cancer optimal care pathway).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Endometrial cancer optimal care pathway

explanation.summary: The 4 mm cut off applies to the first presentation of postmenopausal bleeding. Recurrent bleeding, inadequate sampling, prior tamoxifen exposure, and poor ultrasound visualisation of the midline all defeat the negative predictive value of a thin endometrium. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is required to exclude focal lesions, cornual pathology, and non endometrial sources such as endocervical carcinoma. Blind Pipelle repeat adds little.
key_points: The 4 mm cut off is for a single presentation, not recurrent PMB.
Tamoxifen sub endometrial pathology can be missed by TVUS and Pipelle.
Recurrent PMB equals hysteroscopy regardless of endometrial thickness.
explanation.pearls: Tamoxifen produces sub endometrial cystic change that can mask focal lesions; recurrent PMB in tamoxifen users goes to hysteroscopy without a further Pipelle.
