stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 28 year old G2P0 with one prior first trimester miscarriage presents to the early pregnancy assessment service. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She has had 3 days of mild right iliac fossa discomfort and one episode of light brown vaginal spotting.

She is haemodynamically stable and pain is well controlled with paracetamol. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. She lives locally with reliable transport and phone contact.

On examination her abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Cervix is closed on speculum. Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 2.4 cm right adnexal mass without visible foetal cardiac activity, and no free fluid. Serum beta hCG is 2100 IU/L and has plateaued on two consecutive samples 48 hours apart.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/74, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen; mild right iliac fossa tenderness; no peritonism; cervix closed
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: empty uterus; 2.4 cm right adnexal mass; no foetal cardiac activity; no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Serial serum bhCG 2100 IU/L, plateaued over 48 h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Salpingectomy via diagnostic laparoscopy as definitive surgical management within 24 hours
options.rationale: Surgery is required for tubal ectopic with rupture, haemodynamic instability, foetal cardiac activity, mass at or above 3.5 cm, significant pain, or bhCG at or above 5000 IU/L; none of these apply here (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Suction dilatation and curettage under general anaesthesia to confirm the diagnosis histologically
options.rationale: Dilatation and curettage is not indicated in a woman with a clear ectopic on ultrasound; it delays definitive management and risks disrupting a viable intrauterine pregnancy if the location were uncertain (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management with weekly serum beta hCG measurement until the value falls below 15
options.rationale: Expectant management may be considered when bhCG is under 1000 to 1500 and clearly falling; a plateaued bhCG of 2100 excludes expectant management (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Salpingostomy at laparoscopy to preserve tubal function for future fertility considerations
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is an option in surgical management when the contralateral tube is diseased or absent; medical management remains appropriate here without a surgical indication (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area
options.rationale: Methotrexate is appropriate when bhCG is under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, pain minimal, no rupture, and reliable follow up is possible; all criteria are met here (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

explanation.summary: Ectopic pregnancy management stratifies by clinical stability, ultrasound features, bhCG, and reliability of follow up. Surgical management is required for rupture, instability, foetal cardiac activity, mass at or above 3.5 cm, significant pain, or bhCG at or above 5000. Methotrexate is offered when all these are absent and follow up is reliable. Expectant management is considered for clearly falling low bhCG values. Rh negative women receive anti D.
key_points: Surgical threshold: bhCG at or above 5000 or mass at or above 3.5 cm.
Methotrexate needs bhCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, no rupture, reliable follow up.
Expectant only for clearly falling low bhCG.
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG methotrexate ceiling is bhCG under 5000 IU/L; at or above 5000 the treatment failure rate is unacceptable and surgical management is preferred.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 32 year old G3P0 attends theatre for laparoscopic management of a right tubal ectopic. She had a left salpingectomy 4 years ago for a ruptured left tubal ectopic. Her current pregnancy was spontaneously conceived after 18 months of trying and she strongly wishes to preserve fertility.

At today's laparoscopy the right tube contains a 3.8 cm unruptured ectopic in the ampullary region with an intact serosa and no active bleeding. The left side confirms absent left tube. The uterus and ovaries appear normal. Preoperative bhCG was 7200 IU/L.

data_table.Operative findings: Right ampullary unruptured 3.8 cm ectopic; intact serosa; no bleeding; left tube absent; normal uterus and ovaries
data_table.Reproductive history: 18 months to conceive spontaneously; strongly wishes fertility preservation; prior left salpingectomy 4 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Right salpingectomy because the tube is the only remaining tube and future ectopic risk is high
options.rationale: Removing the only remaining tube commits her to IVF; when the tube is the only tube and the ectopic is amenable to salpingostomy without extensive tubal damage, the RANZCOG position is that salpingostomy is preferred to preserve any chance of natural conception even accepting the elevated recurrent ectopic risk (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Right salpingostomy with removal of the products and preservation of the tube for future fertility
options.rationale: When the contralateral tube is absent, salpingostomy is preferred over salpingectomy because it preserves the only remaining tube and any chance of natural conception; postoperative bhCG monitoring is required until non pregnant, and about one in five need methotrexate for persistent trophoblast (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Abandon surgery and give single dose intramuscular methotrexate given fertility preservation intent
options.rationale: Methotrexate is contraindicated with bhCG at or above 5000 and mass at or above 3.5 cm because treatment failure and rupture rates are high; a laparoscopy already in progress with a suitable ampullary lesion should proceed to surgical management (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Milk the ectopic out of the fimbrial end of the tube to avoid opening the tube or removing it
options.rationale: Fimbrial expression is only appropriate for the small subset of distal fimbrial ectopics presenting at the fimbrial end; ampullary lesions require salpingostomy or salpingectomy because expression risks incomplete removal and recurrent bleeding (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Ipsilateral cornual resection with removal of the uterine horn to prevent recurrent ipsilateral ectopic
options.rationale: Cornual resection is reserved for interstitial ectopics; this is an ampullary ectopic and cornual resection would inappropriately compromise the uterus (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

explanation.summary: Choice between salpingectomy and salpingostomy depends on the state of the contralateral tube. When the contralateral tube is normal, salpingectomy is preferred because subsequent pregnancy rates are similar and recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk is avoided. When the contralateral tube is diseased or absent, salpingostomy is preferred to preserve any chance of natural conception. Salpingostomy requires postoperative bhCG monitoring to detect the roughly 1 in 5 cases of persistent trophoblast which need salvage methotrexate.
key_points: Normal contralateral tube: salpingectomy.
Absent or diseased contralateral tube: salpingostomy.
Post salpingostomy: weekly bhCG until under 5 IU/L; methotrexate for persistent trophoblast.
explanation.pearls: The historical bilaterality flip: a prior contralateral salpingectomy converts the standard salpingectomy answer to salpingostomy because the affected tube is now the only remaining tube.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy
RCOG Green top guideline 21 Ectopic pregnancy

stem:
You are the early pregnancy assessment service registrar. A 26 year old G1P0 presents at an estimated 5+3 weeks gestation with 24 hours of very light brown vaginal spotting. She has no pain and has been afebrile.

She is haemodynamically well. She lives 15 minutes from the hospital and has reliable phone contact and transport. She has no significant medical history and takes only a pregnancy multivitamin.

Abdomen is soft and non tender. Speculum shows a closed cervix with a small amount of dark blood. Vital signs are within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a small 1.2 cm left adnexal mass with no yolk sac or foetal pole, and no free fluid. Serum bhCG on presentation is 480 IU/L and a repeat 48 hours later is 320 IU/L.

data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen; cervix closed; small dark blood on speculum
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: empty uterus; 1.2 cm left adnexal mass; no yolk sac or foetal pole; no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG day 0 480 IU/L; day 2 320 IU/L (falling)
data_table.Social: Lives 15 min from hospital; reliable transport and phone contact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial serum beta hCG measurement every 48 to 72 hours until under 15
options.rationale: Expectant management is appropriate when the woman is pain free and stable, bhCG is under about 1500 and falling by at least 15% over 48 hours, mass is small with no cardiac activity, and follow up is reliable; all criteria are met here (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area
options.rationale: Methotrexate is appropriate for stable plateaued or slowly rising bhCG under 5000; when bhCG is under 1500 and clearly falling with reliable follow up, expectant management avoids methotrexate toxicity (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy today with proceed to salpingectomy or salpingostomy as indicated
options.rationale: Surgery is required for instability, rupture, cardiac activity, mass at or above 3.5 cm, significant pain, or bhCG at or above 5000; none apply here (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Admit for 48 hour inpatient observation with intravenous cannula and serial abdominal examinations
options.rationale: Inpatient observation is unnecessary for a stable pain free woman with falling bhCG and reliable follow up; outpatient serial bhCG is safe and appropriate (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Suction dilatation and curettage to confirm absence of intrauterine pregnancy before further decisions
options.rationale: Ultrasound already shows an empty uterus and a probable adnexal ectopic; dilatation and curettage adds no diagnostic value here (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

explanation.summary: Expectant management of tubal ectopic is appropriate when the woman is pain free and haemodynamically stable, bhCG is under 1000 to 1500 and clearly falling by at least 15% over 48 hours, mass is under 3 cm with no cardiac activity, and follow up is reliable. Serial bhCG is measured every 48 to 72 hours until under 15 IU/L. Around 30 to 40% of ectopics selected on these criteria resolve without intervention.
key_points: Expectant: bhCG under 1500 and falling, small mass, no pain, reliable follow up.
Methotrexate: bhCG under 5000 and static or slow rise.
Surgery: bhCG at or above 5000, mass at or above 3.5 cm, pain, cardiac activity, rupture.
explanation.pearls: The three thresholds worth memorising for ectopic pathway choice: bhCG 1500 for expectant, 5000 for methotrexate ceiling, and 3.5 cm mass or cardiac activity for surgery.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Severe features and MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis
stem:
You are the birthing suite registrar. A 32 year old primigravida at 35+2 weeks presents with a 6 hour history of severe headache unresponsive to paracetamol and new epigastric pain. She reports blurred vision this morning.

Her antenatal course was uncomplicated with normal 20 week anatomy scan and normal midtrimester blood pressure readings. She takes no medications.

She is alert and oriented. Reflexes are brisk with three beats of clonus. Abdomen shows mild epigastric tenderness. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 172/108, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8, foetal heart rate 145 reactive. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. Bloods: platelets 82 x10^9/L (150 to 400), ALT 145 U/L (under 35), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45 to 90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.35).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 172/108, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.8, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Alert; brisk reflexes with 3 beats clonus; mild epigastric tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick 3+ protein; platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 145 U/L (<35); creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35)
data_table.Obstetric history: Primigravida at 35+2; uncomplicated antenatal course; normal midtrimester BPs

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated every 10 minutes until blood pressure controlled
options.rationale: Blood pressure control with intravenous labetalol is important and should occur in parallel, but the single most important intervention to prevent immediate maternal death is seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in pregnancy guideline).

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia to remove the placenta as trigger
options.rationale: Delivery is the definitive treatment and will occur but not before magnesium and blood pressure control; category 1 caesarean under general anaesthesia in an unstable pre eclamptic risks intracerebral haemorrhage from the pressor response to intubation (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in pregnancy guideline).

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion
options.rationale: Severe pre eclampsia with neurological symptoms, clonus, HELLP features, and severe hypertension carries imminent risk of eclamptic seizure; magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g per hour is the single most important intervention to prevent eclampsia and reduce maternal mortality (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in pregnancy guideline).

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg every 12 hours to accelerate platelet recovery in HELLP syndrome
options.rationale: Dexamethasone in HELLP has not shown maternal or perinatal benefit outside of foetal lung maturation and is not the immediate priority (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in pregnancy guideline).

options.text: Platelet transfusion targeting a count above 100 before proceeding to any intervention or delivery
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is not indicated at 82 in the absence of bleeding or planned neuraxial anaesthesia; the immediate priority is seizure prophylaxis (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in pregnancy guideline).

explanation.summary: Severe pre eclampsia is defined by severe hypertension at or above 160/110, headache, visual disturbance, clonus, epigastric pain, thrombocytopenia under 100, or transaminase over twice normal. Management priorities are magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, blood pressure control with labetalol or hydralazine, and expedited delivery. Magnesium sulfate is the intervention that reduces maternal mortality and eclampsia rates in randomised trials (MAGPIE).
key_points: MgSO4 4 g load then 1 g per hour reduces eclampsia and maternal death.
Severe hypertension at or above 160/110 needs urgent IV antihypertensive.
Delivery is definitive but should be timed after stabilisation.
explanation.pearls: In severe pre eclampsia magnesium goes up before delivery is planned; MAGPIE showed a halving of eclamptic seizures with the 4 g load and 1 g per hour infusion.

stem:
You are the birthing suite registrar. A 34 year old G4P3 has just delivered a 4.1 kg baby vaginally after a prolonged second stage. Estimated blood loss now stands at 1200 mL with ongoing brisk fresh loss.

Her antenatal course was complicated by pre eclampsia treated with oral labetalol from 32 weeks. Blood pressure on admission today was 152/98. She has known aspirin sensitive asthma and a documented severe reaction to ergometrine during a prior postpartum haemorrhage.

On examination the uterus is boggy at the umbilicus. Placenta appears intact on inspection and the perineum has a small first degree tear only. Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 138/88, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% room air, temp 36.8. Oxytocin 10 units intramuscular has been given as active management of the third stage and a further oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours has been commenced. Bimanual uterine massage has begun and a repeat firm fundal massage now returns the uterus toward normal tone.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 138/88, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy at umbilicus, tone improving with bimanual massage; placenta appears complete; small first degree perineal tear
data_table.Medications given: Oxytocin 10 units IM at third stage; oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 h infusion running
data_table.History: Pre eclampsia on labetalol; aspirin sensitive asthma; documented severe prior reaction to ergometrine

lead_in: Which additional uterotonic is most appropriate next?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular repeated every 2 to 4 hours until bleeding controlled
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated by prior severe reaction and by significant hypertension in pregnancy; both apply here (Source: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Carboprost 250 mcg intramuscular every 15 minutes to a maximum cumulative dose of 2 mg
options.rationale: Carboprost is a synthetic prostaglandin F2 alpha with potent bronchoconstrictor activity and is contraindicated in asthma; aspirin sensitive asthma marks a subgroup at particularly high risk of severe bronchospasm (Source: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes as the next uterotonic to control the bleeding
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and should be given early in postpartum haemorrhage but it is not a uterotonic; both are given in parallel, not as uterotonic replacements for each other (Source: WOMAN trial Lancet 2017).

options.text: Misoprostol 800 mcg per rectum as a single dose in addition to the current oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: With ergometrine and carboprost both contraindicated, misoprostol 800 mcg rectally is the appropriate second line uterotonic; it is a PGE1 analogue and does not have the bronchoconstrictor or hypertensive risks (Source: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage; WHO Recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage
WHO Recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Second oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours in addition to the first
options.rationale: Escalating to a second oxytocin infusion adds fluid load and risks hyponatraemia without additional uterotonic effect once maximal receptor occupancy is reached; the appropriate step is a different class of uterotonic (Source: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Uterotonic escalation in postpartum haemorrhage follows a class ladder. Oxytocin is first line. Ergometrine is second line but contraindicated in hypertension and previous adverse reaction. Carboprost is a potent PGF2 alpha but contraindicated in asthma. Misoprostol is a PGE1 analogue safe in both hypertension and asthma. Tranexamic acid is given early alongside uterotonics per the WOMAN trial and is not a uterotonic.
key_points: Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension.
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma.
Misoprostol is safe when both above are excluded.
explanation.pearls: The uterotonic decision tree in PPH branches on hypertension (blocks ergometrine) and asthma (blocks carboprost); when both apply, misoprostol 800 mcg rectally is the escape.

sources.label: RANZCOG Prevention detection and management of subsequent postpartum haemorrhage
WHO Recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: Late preterm steroids and asymptomatic bacteriuria
stem:
You are the antenatal ward registrar. A 26 year old G1 at 32+4 weeks with confirmed preterm labour has been admitted. Cervical examination shows 2 cm dilatation and 60% effacement. Membranes are intact.

Her antenatal course has been unremarkable and she has no medical conditions. She takes only pregnancy multivitamins.

Abdomen is soft between contractions and non tender. Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, foetal heart rate 145 reactive. Midstream urine sent yesterday for asymptomatic screening has returned pure growth of Escherichia coli at 10^8 colony forming units per litre with sensitivity to cefalexin, nitrofurantoin, and trimethoprim.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 2 cm dilated 60% effaced; membranes intact; soft non tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: MSU: pure E coli 10^8 CFU/L; sensitive to cefalexin, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim

lead_in: Which combination of interventions is most appropriate?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated at 24 hours, no antibiotic given culture reflects colonisation
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy at 10^8 CFU/L is treated with antibiotics because untreated bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis in around 30% of pregnancies and increases preterm birth risk (Source: eTG Antibiotic; RANZCOG Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy).

options.text: No corticosteroids since gestation is beyond 32 weeks and cefalexin 500 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days
options.rationale: Antenatal steroids are indicated up to 34+6 weeks with imminent risk of preterm birth; 32+4 weeks is well within the window and steroid benefit is substantial (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal corticosteroids).

options.text: Dexamethasone 6 mg intramuscular repeated 4 times plus nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 7 days
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is an alternative to betamethasone but the standard Australian first line is betamethasone; nitrofurantoin is avoided within 4 weeks of birth because of neonatal haemolysis risk in G6PD deficiency and this woman is at imminent risk of preterm birth (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal corticosteroids; AMH).

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated at 24 hours plus trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist avoided in the first trimester and is not first line in Australian pregnancy guidance despite sensitivity on culture (Source: eTG Antibiotic; AMH).

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated at 24 hours plus cefalexin 500 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days
options.rationale: Betamethasone is indicated to reduce respiratory distress syndrome and other preterm morbidity between 24 and 34+6 weeks with imminent risk of birth; asymptomatic bacteriuria at 10^8 CFU/L is treated with cefalexin 500 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 to 7 days as first line in Australian guidance (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal corticosteroids; eTG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, and mortality when given between 24 and 34+6 weeks with anticipated preterm birth within 7 days. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular is repeated at 24 hours. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is defined at 10^8 CFU/L or higher and is treated because of progression to pyelonephritis and association with preterm birth. Cefalexin is the usual Australian first line; nitrofurantoin is avoided close to birth.
key_points: Steroids: 24 to 34+6 weeks, imminent birth within 7 days.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is always treated.
Cefalexin first line; nitrofurantoin avoided close to birth.
explanation.pearls: Betamethasone in Australian obstetrics is 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated once at 24 hours; the 34+6 ceiling is the Australian cut off, above which routine steroids are not standard.

subtopic_detail: Perimenopausal HMB with fibroids and IUS choice
stem:
You are the gynaecology clinic registrar. A 47 year old woman presents with 18 months of increasingly heavy predictable periods. She has completed her family and does not wish to conceive again.

Her BMI is 28 with no other medical conditions. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and cervical screening is up to date.

Bimanual examination reveals a bulky irregular uterus corresponding to 12 weeks gestation size. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an anteverted uterus with multiple intramural fibroids the largest measuring 4 cm, no submucosal component distorting the endometrial cavity, and an endometrium of 8 mm. Uterine cavity length is 10 cm. Full blood count reveals haemoglobin 102 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 76 fL (80 to 100), and ferritin 6 microgram/L (15 to 200). Cervical screening and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Bulky irregular uterus 12 week size on bimanual
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: anteverted uterus; multiple intramural fibroids largest 4 cm; no submucosal component distorting cavity; endometrium 8 mm; cavity length 10 cm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (115-165); MCV 76 fL (80-100); ferritin 6 mcg/L (15-200); cervical screen negative; TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system after outpatient endometrial biopsy to exclude hyperplasia
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective first line pharmacological treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding including with fibroids that do not distort the cavity and a cavity length under 12 cm; endometrial biopsy is done first because she is over 45 with prolonged HMB per RANZCOG (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation as a fertility sparing option that avoids surgical morbidity of hysterectomy
options.rationale: Uterine artery embolisation is considered for symptomatic fibroids after less invasive options have failed; it is not first line and fertility sparing is not a driver here as family is complete (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy as definitive management for perimenopausal HMB
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but is not first line; medical management and less invasive options are tried first unless there is a specific indication such as failed medical therapy or suspected malignancy (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Endometrial ablation using bipolar radiofrequency as a definitive uterine preserving procedure now
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation is contraindicated with a distorted cavity or cavity length beyond 10 to 12 cm; large intramural fibroids and a 10 cm cavity length also make ablation less effective and Mirena is preferred first line (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 5 mg orally daily for 3 months as a selective progesterone receptor modulator now
options.rationale: Ulipristal for fibroids has been withdrawn from routine use in Australia because of hepatotoxicity signals and is not first line for heavy menstrual bleeding (Source: TGA Ulipristal acetate safety advisory).

explanation.summary: The Mirena levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss by around 90% and is first line pharmacological therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding including with intramural fibroids provided the cavity is not distorted and length is under 12 cm. Endometrial sampling is required first in women over 45 with prolonged or new heavy menstrual bleeding to exclude hyperplasia or malignancy. Hysterectomy, ablation, and uterine artery embolisation are reserved for treatment failure or specific indications.
key_points: Mirena is first line for HMB even with intramural fibroids not distorting the cavity.
Endometrial sampling required before Mirena in over 45s.
Ablation contraindicated with distorted cavity or length over 12 cm.
explanation.pearls: The Mirena cavity length limit is around 12 cm; measure the sound before inserting and always sample the endometrium first in women over 45 with heavy menstrual bleeding.
